note: Cellgrimage clue bank (What the Cell, original). Answers are Name|tier|alias. Tier 1 = most common, 5 = rare but correct. names:true lets a surname match.

specimens.name: Human blood cells
specimens.desc: Red blood cells (the dimpled discs), a white blood cell (round and bumpy) and small platelets, seen with a scanning electron microscope.
specimens.credit: Bruce Wetzel and Harry Schaefer, National Cancer Institute (public domain)

specimens.name: Cilia lining an airway
specimens.desc: Ciliated cells lining a bronchiole in the lungs. Their cilia beat together to sweep mucus and trapped particles up and out of the airways. Scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: E. coli dividing
specimens.desc: An Escherichia coli bacterium dividing in two by binary fission. Each cell is about 2 micrometres long. Scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: CDC / Evangeline Sowers and Janice Haney Carr (public domain)

specimens.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
specimens.desc: The rod-shaped bacteria that cause tuberculosis, a lung disease spread through the air. Scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: CDC / Ray Butler and Janice Carr (public domain)

specimens.name: HIV leaving an infected white blood cell
specimens.desc: New HIV particles (coloured green) budding from an infected lymphocyte. HIV destroys helper T cells, which weakens the immune system. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: CDC / C. Goldsmith, P. Feorino, E. L. Palmer and W. R. McManus (public domain)

specimens.name: A cell infected with SARS-CoV-2
specimens.desc: A cell covered in SARS-CoV-2 particles, the virus that causes COVID-19. The colours were added to tell the virus and the cell apart. Scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: NIAID, National Institutes of Health (public domain)

specimens.name: Influenza virus
specimens.desc: A single influenza virus particle. Its outer envelope comes from the membrane of the host cell it left, and it carries its genes as RNA. Coloured transmission electron micrograph.

specimens.name: Pollen grains
specimens.desc: Pollen from several common plants, including sunflower, morning glory and lily. Spiky, sculpted walls help many grains cling to insect pollinators. Scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility (public domain)

specimens.name: A stoma on a tomato leaf
specimens.desc: A pore in the leaf surface between two guard cells. Stomata open to let carbon dioxide in, and water vapour escapes through them in transpiration. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: Diatoms
specimens.desc: Single-celled algae with intricate cell walls made of silica (glass). As producers, diatoms make a large share of the oxygen released in the oceans. Light micrograph.
specimens.credit: Gordon T. Taylor, Stony Brook University (public domain)

specimens.name: Budding yeast
specimens.desc: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the yeast used in baking and brewing. New cells grow as buds from the parent cell. Light micrograph.

specimens.name: Skeletal muscle
specimens.desc: Muscle fibres seen with a transmission electron microscope. The repeating dark and light bands are sarcomeres, which shorten as myosin pulls on actin.

specimens.name: Malaria parasites in red blood cells
specimens.desc: Plasmodium falciparum parasites (the small purple dots) inside red blood cells. Plasmodium is a single-celled protist spread by mosquitoes. Stained light micrograph.

specimens.name: A slice through a plant stem
specimens.desc: A stained slice through the stem of a squash plant (Cucurbita), showing the tissues that carry water and sugars. Light micrograph.
specimens.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library (CC0)

specimens.name: Staphylococcus aureus
specimens.desc: Round bacteria (cocci) that grow in grape-like clusters. Antibiotic-resistant strains such as MRSA are a serious problem in hospitals. Scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: CDC / Janice Carr and Matthew Arduino (public domain)

specimens.name: Bacillus anthracis
specimens.desc: Rod-shaped bacteria in long chains, stained purple by Gram staining. Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax and can survive for years as spores. Light micrograph.

specimens.name: Chlamydomonas, a green alga
specimens.desc: A single-celled green alga. Its large cup-shaped chloroplast, packed with thylakoids, fills much of the cell. Transmission electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility (public domain)

specimens.name: A white blood cell engulfing bacteria
specimens.desc: A neutrophil (green) engulfing MRSA bacteria (purple) by phagocytosis. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: NIAID, National Institutes of Health (public domain)

specimens.name: Salmonella invading human cells
specimens.desc: Salmonella bacteria (red) invading cultured human cells. Salmonella is a common cause of food poisoning. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.
specimens.credit: Rocky Mountain Laboratories, NIAID, NIH (public domain)

specimens.name: Ebola virus
specimens.desc: A long, thread-like Ebola virus particle, curled at one end into a shepherd's-crook shape. Ebola spreads through contact with body fluids. Transmission electron micrograph.

specimens.name: A flea
specimens.desc: A flea, a wingless insect that feeds on blood. Its flattened body and long back legs suit life among fur, and fleas can carry the plague bacterium. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: The mouthparts of an aphid
specimens.desc: The head of an aphid with its needle-like mouthparts (stylet). Aphids push the stylet into phloem sieve tubes and feed on the sugary sap. Scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: A fruit fly's compound eye
specimens.desc: Part of the compound eye of a fruit fly. It is made of hundreds of units, each with its own lens, with sensory bristles between them. Scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: Anabaena, a cyanobacterium
specimens.desc: A curled chain of Anabaena cells. These bacteria photosynthesise, and some cells in the chain can also fix nitrogen from the air. Light micrograph.

specimens.name: Spirogyra, a green alga
specimens.desc: A filament of Spirogyra cells. Each cell has a ribbon-shaped chloroplast wound in a spiral, which gives the alga its name. Light micrograph.

specimens.name: Trypanosomes in blood
specimens.desc: Trypanosoma cruzi parasites (the purple, wavy cells) among red blood cells. This flagellated protist causes Chagas disease and is spread by insects. Stained light micrograph.

specimens.name: Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum
specimens.desc: Purkinje cells from the cerebellum: large neurons, each with a rounded cell body and a densely branched tree of dendrites. Stained light micrograph.

specimens.name: Onion root tip cells dividing
specimens.desc: Cells near the tip of an onion root, where cells divide by mitosis. Most cells are in interphase, but some show condensed chromosomes. Stained light micrograph.
specimens.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library (CC0)

specimens.name: A lymphocyte
specimens.desc: A lymphocyte, the kind of white blood cell that makes antibodies (B cells) or destroys infected cells (T cells). Its surface is covered in tiny projections. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: Measles virus
specimens.desc: A measles virus particle, cut through to show the coiled RNA inside its envelope. Measles spreads very easily, but vaccination prevents it. Transmission electron micrograph.

specimens.name: Aspergillus mould
specimens.desc: Spore-bearing heads of the mould Aspergillus, stained blue. Each round head releases thousands of tiny spores into the air. Like other moulds, it is a saprotroph. Light micrograph.

specimens.name: A Vibrio bacterium with flagella
specimens.desc: A Vibrio vulnificus bacterium (green) with its whip-like flagella, which it uses to swim. Vibrio species live in warm seawater. Coloured scanning electron micrograph.

specimens.name: Hairs on a leaf
specimens.desc: Hairs (trichomes) on a leaf surface. They trap a layer of still, moist air that slows water loss, and some help to put off insects. Scanning electron micrograph.
